[Scishow interview with Doug Emlen](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=CyidhY2dc5I) 14+ minutes.

In the interview Emlen discusses what, if anything, he thinks we can learn from the evolution of animal weaponry (he notes that he is a biologist, not a military historian and that his interpretation is simply a thought experiment). His basic premise is that species who develop large, otherwise bulky weapons, are the species who engage in duels. When animals fight each other one on one, the bigger weapon wins, where as the species who get into all out brawls don't tend to develop these kinds of weapons as the fights are chaotic and something like huge horns doesn't necessarily convey an advantage if you're getting attacked from all sides.

He links this point in a number of interesting ways to how cultures can act in the same way. When powers face each other head on they tend to enter arms races. The example used most predominantly in the interview is The Cold War where the US and USSR essentially engaged in a political duel and all of their technologies got swept up in this arms race.

His concluding point is that in the animal world, when the weapons these animals develop become too large for other members on the species to compete, what you see is essentially 'cheating' start to take place. If they can't possible fight you head on, they find a way to go around you and avoid the fight as much as possible; they stop playing by the rules. He connects this to the way we see wars in the Middle East play out where bands of guerilla fighters use unconventional or even illegal means to fight a much stronger opponent. IEDs, dressing as/hiding amongst civilians and suicide bombings may be examples of the enemy 'cheating' as they don't posses the means to take us head on. It ends up leading him to an unsettling conclusion.

I just thought this was an interesting perspective and one worth noticing.
